description: We are interested in the study of space and planets, as well as the collection of data regarding them. The goal of our project is to provide reliable information about the planets and objects within the solar system. We are looking for team members with skills in programming and design.
summary:
Space for Young Explorers: Left Behind, Not Forgotten
We built a free, interactive website that teaches children about the NASA spacecraft and equipment humanity has left in space: laser reflectors and rovers on the Moon, landers and rovers on Mars, and probes like Voyager 1 that are still flying beyond the planets. Children find each machine at its real landing site in the “Space Archaeologist” game, open 24 spacecraft cards with NASA photos, and hear every machine tell its own story aloud. This answers the “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge by turning “abandoned” hardware into living stories. It matters because these machines are still teaching us: laser reflectors left by Apollo show the Moon drifts 3.8 cm a year, and this week Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth.
details:
What it does. The site opens with “Left Behind in Space”: a live countdown to Voyager 1 reaching one light-day (November 18, 2026) and three entry points:
Left Behind in Space: 24 cards (Apollo reflectors, lunar rovers, Surveyor 3, Viking, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity, Pioneer, Voyager, New Horizons, Cassini and more). Each card explains where the machine is, why it was sent, what we learned and its status today, with NASA photos and a “Listen” button where the spacecraft speaks in the first person.
Space Archaeologist: a game on maps of the Moon and Mars. Players send signals, see the latitude and longitude of each try, and find artifacts at their real landing sites (for example, Ingenuity in Jezero Crater, 18.4°N 77.5°E).
Letters from Space: a comic narrated by the spacecraft themselves.
The site also has a quiz about left-behind technology, a missions timeline, planet explorer, weight calculator, glossary, a rank system (Cadet and up), and three 3D games: Lunar Frontier, Shards of Pluto 3D and Ash of Orbit (12+, with an in-game NASA Field Guide).
How it works. The whole project is a single HTML file that runs in any browser, even offline: it works from a USB stick in a school with no internet (only the NASA photos, web fonts and the Pluto 3D game need a connection). Planet textures are generated with code, and narration uses the browser’s built-in speech synthesis. It works on phones, and it has text-size, sound and light/dark theme settings for accessibility.
Benefits. It gives children a reason to care about space history, connects them to a real event happening this week, and teaches real geography of the Moon and Mars through play.
Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG, Canvas, WebGL (three.js), Web Speech API; the Lunar Frontier game uses React and Tailwind CSS. The comics were drawn with Gemini; every AI image carries a visible “AI-generated” label.
